chapter_theme: The surfeit of lonely grief turns into an argument about reciprocity. Mutual love is the seedless fruit and the timely rain; one-sided love is a carrying pole weighted at one end. The chapter asks what love is worth if it isn't returned.
structure_note: All ten are the woman's. She starts with a run on mutuality (1191-1196), blames the love god (1197), and then turns to the absence of any word from him (1198-1200). Parimelazhagar's headnotes treat 1198 and 1200 as about a message that doesn't come.

1191.reading: The woman says those who are loved by the ones they love have obtained the stoneless fruit of love.
1191.nuance: A fruit without a stone is enjoyment with nothing to spit out. The verse is general and ungendered, while Parimelazhagar makes it 'women loved by husbands', adds that this needs good deeds from before, and supplies the unstated close that she hasn't got this fruit.

1192.reading: The woman says the grace shown by the beloved to the one who loves them is like the rain to those who live by it.
1192.nuance: The grace here is measured and timely, as rain is, and Parimelazhagar takes that to include a man who returns from duty when he should. He brings out the shadow: if the rain fails, those dependent on it die.

1193.reading: The woman says the pride of saying 'we shall live' suits only those who are loved by those they love.
1193.nuance: செருக்கு, 'pride', is usually a vice in the Kural, and here it is a privilege she envies. Parimelazhagar and Manakkudavar agree on the corollary: what suits her is death.

1194.reading: The woman says that those who are esteemed are still without something, if they aren't loved by the one they love.
1194.nuance: Manakkudavar ends with a proverb, கொண்டான் கயிற் கண்டான் காயும்: if the husband is angry at her, all who see her will be too. That gives a social reason why public esteem can't survive this loss.

positions.position: The esteemed one is honoured by chaste women, and கெழீஇயிலர் means she lacks good deeds, that is, she has bad karma.
The esteemed one is honoured by the world, and the word means she becomes one without being desired.
The verse is about the partner who withdraws love, who is then thought to lack the sense of friendship.

1195.reading: The woman asks what those she loves can do for her if they themselves don't love her.
1195.nuance: It answers a compliment. Parimelazhagar has the friend say that she bore this well because of her love; the reply is that love has brought her only pain.

1196.reading: The woman says love is painful when it is on one side only, and sweet on both sides, like the load of a carrying pole.
1196.nuance: It is a physical fact that a load at both ends is easier than half that load at one. The verse therefore doesn't claim only that shared love is pleasant; shared love is also lighter to carry.

1197.reading: The woman asks whether Kaman, who works on one side alone, doesn't see her misery and grief.
1197.nuance: A rare appearance of a named love god in the Kural, and the verse makes him a partial combatant. The older commentators take the theology seriously: for Parimelazhagar, a god should know all and be impartial, and for Manakkudavar, he wouldn't hurt her if he saw, being a god. Kalaignar's version has him as simply indifferent.

1198.reading: The woman says that no one in the world is harder than those who go on living without receiving a kind word from their beloved.
1198.nuance: வன்கண் is ambiguous between hardness and courage, and Pope chooses 'braver'. The commentators read it as an accusation she makes against herself. Parimelazhagar notes that any word at all from him would count as sweet.

1199.reading: The woman says that though the man she longs for gives no grace, even இசை from him is sweet to her ears.

positions.position: இசை means any word at all about him, even that he isn't coming, and she hasn't got even that.
positions.quote: 'அவர் வாரார் என்னுஞ் சொல்லாயினும் அமையும்,' என்பதுபட நின்றது.

positions.position: The word means his fame, and words that praise him are honey to her.

1200.reading: The woman tells her heart that it wants to tell its pain to one who is not close, and that it may as well try to fill up the sea.
1200.nuance: வாழிய, 'may you live', is sarcasm here for Parimelazhagar. The chapter ends with her declining what she spent the chapter wanting, and the sea from 1137 and 1164 comes back as a job to be done with a basket. It is an image of utter futility.

links.note: 11 says that the rain, sustaining the world, is to be known as ambrosia. 1192 uses the whole opening doctrine for one person's survival. The same dependence that the Kural gives to all life at its start reappears as a lover's condition.

Both use the carrying pole (கா). In 1163, love and shame hang at the ends of her life, and the pole is breaking. In 1196, love should hang on both people. The first is a struggle within one self, and the second is a fault between two.

வன்கண் is the same word in both. In 1156 he is hard because he could speak of leaving. In 1198 she calls herself hard for going on living without a word from him. The accusation has moved from him to her.

source_issues: 1191: Manakkudavar's entry has பாலில்லாத where the sense requires பரலில்லாத, 'stoneless'.
1198: Parimelazhagar's entry ends without the usual '---' and its note isn't marked விளக்கம் as elsewhere. This is only a formatting difference.
1200: Parimelazhagar's note has கேட்பார் உறவினராகலானும், where the logic needs கேட்பார் உறவிலராகலானும். It looks like a corruption.
